buildings.name: The Rollins
buildings.note: Essex Crossing flagship. Trader Joe's and Target in the retail base — the most self-contained building on the list.

buildings.name: The Suffolk
buildings.note: Rooftop pool and fitness club. Three floors are Abode micro-units at 315–350 sq ft — confirm which layout you're touring.

buildings.name: The Essex
buildings.note: One of the tallest on the LES. Sits directly on Delancey, which is the loudest stretch in the neighborhood.

buildings.name: The Artisan
buildings.note: Largest building in the Essex Crossing plan; rentals start on the sixth floor. VITAL climbing gym downstairs.

buildings.name: The Ludlow
buildings.note: Next door to Katz's on the busiest nightlife block downtown. Valet service and a yoga/Pilates studio.

buildings.name: The Chrystie
buildings.note: Arquitectonica and SLCE. Recently renovated, and on the Bowery side rather than deep in the LES.

buildings.name: Sioné
buildings.note: Loft-scale windows, white oak floors, smart entry and thermostats. Walnut cabinetry and Bosch appliances.

buildings.name: Jones L.E.S.
buildings.note: Condo-quality finishes — soaking tubs, custom Italian cabinetry. Roof terrace has an outdoor screening area.

buildings.name: 155 Attorney Street
buildings.note: Boutique. Virtual doorman rather than a staffed desk — worth knowing if package handling matters to you.

buildings.name: The Orchard
buildings.note: Small and discreet at Orchard & Delancey. Private outdoor space in every apartment.

buildings.name: Stella LES
buildings.note: On the EV/LES seam. Keyless entry and in-duct air purification; resident reviews are hard on management.

buildings.name: Gotham Court
buildings.note: Small doorman mid-rise with high ceilings, a block off Houston.

buildings.name: 275 South Street
buildings.note: Converted post-war high-rise with East River and Brooklyn views. Renovated interiors, frequent leasing specials.

buildings.name: The Madison Jackson
buildings.note: Far southeast corner of the neighborhood, near the bridges. One of the few LES buildings with a pool.

buildings.name: The Norfolk
buildings.note: 2023-built tower near Grand St, paired with Gotham Organization's 64 Norfolk senior housing next door. No staffed doorman.

buildings.name: EVGB
buildings.note: Extell. A 19,000 sq ft roof deck with fire pits, plus a pool. Target and Trader Joe's are steps away.

buildings.name: 2 Cooper Square
buildings.note: Astor Place edge — the best transit access of anything downtown on this list. Roof deck with a swimming pool.

buildings.name: The Nathaniel
buildings.note: E 12th near Third Ave, which reads more Gramercy than East Village. Courtyard, reflecting pool, club lounge.

buildings.name: Steiner East Village
buildings.note: Condo at Ave A & E 12th; units come up as rentals through owners. Concierge, but no leasing office to walk into.

buildings.name: Avalon Bowery Place I
buildings.note: 2007 vintage but generous floorplates and a deep amenity package. Arguably the most polished block in the EV.

buildings.name: Avalon Bowery Place II
buildings.note: Smaller sibling across the street, sharing the Bowery Place location without the garage.

buildings.name: Eleventh & Third
buildings.note: Boutique, renovated 2014 — concrete counters, walnut floors. Recent reviews say new management cut the night doorman.

buildings.name: The Adele
buildings.note: Deep in Alphabet City near Ave C. Rooftop with a lawn and panoramic views, but a 15-minute walk to a train.

buildings.name: 250 E Houston (Red Square)
buildings.note: The Tibor Kalman clock building, renovated throughout. Wi-Fi lounge with a private conference room.

buildings.name: 152 Second Avenue
buildings.note: Paris Forino interiors — whitewashed oak, limed brick, private balconies. Small and quiet.

buildings.name: EVE
buildings.note: Trader Joe's is the retail tenant. Scandinavian-leaning interiors, courtyard, pet grooming station.

buildings.name: Arabella 101
buildings.note: Far east on Ave D. LEED certified, skyline views, herb garden on the roof. Residents rate the staff highly.

buildings.name: Bloom 62
buildings.note: Post-war mid-rise on Ave B facing Tompkins Square. Doorman and gym, modest amenity set.

buildings.name: Deco East
buildings.note: Doorman mid-rise where rent includes heat and hot water — rare at this tier.

buildings.name: CD280
buildings.note: Studios and one-bedrooms only, with rent-stabilized units in the mix. Unusual value for the amenity level.

buildings.name: The Sky East
buildings.note: Doorman mid-rise deep in Alphabet City, near the Ave C corridor.

buildings.name: Tompkins Square Plaza
buildings.note: Two towers separated by a plaza and fountain — a rare setback from the street in this part of the EV.

buildings.name: The Hudson East
buildings.note: Mixed-income building with rooftop terraces, rear garden patios, and duplex live/work spaces.

buildings.name: Eastville Gardens
buildings.note: Quiet block between Aves B and C. Doorman elevator building with a gym.

buildings.name: The Houston
buildings.note: Hill West infill between Aves A and B; 40 of the 157 units are income-restricted. Virtual doorman rather than a staffed desk.

buildings.name: The East
buildings.note: Madison Realty Capital tower next to the Con Ed plant near Ave C; 30% of the 196 units are set aside as affordable.

buildings.name: 298 Mulberry
buildings.note: One of only two real doorman rentals in Nolita — historic-district rules kept everything else low-rise walk-ups. Staff reviews are exceptional.

buildings.name: 227 Mulberry
buildings.note: The other one. Doorman elevator building with a gym, in the middle of the Mulberry restaurant strip.

buildings.name: Mulberry House
buildings.note: SHoP Architects-designed with a rippling brown-brick facade, directly across from the landmark Puck Building. A genuine third Nolita doorman rental, but with only 8 full-floor loft units, vacancies are rare.

buildings.name: The Soho Abbey
buildings.note: Despite the "SoHo" marketing name, its Mott/Houston/Elizabeth corner address places it firmly in Nolita — one of the largest doorman buildings in the immediate area. No pets allowed.

buildings.name: SPRING
buildings.note: Originally the 1927 East River Savings Bank designed by Cass Gilbert, converted to residential in 2004 with its Beaux-Arts limestone facade intact. Sits on Nolita's western edge, so some sites file it under SoHo.

buildings.name: Nolita Place Condominiums
buildings.note: Fronts Bowery, Nolita's eastern boundary, which is why some sites tag it Lower East Side instead. Some units have unusually large private terraces — up to roughly 760 sq ft.

buildings.name: The Archive
buildings.note: Landmark warehouse conversion taking the whole block — double-height arched windows, high ceilings, and by far the largest inventory in the West Village.

buildings.name: 600 Washington
buildings.note: Part of the Morton Square complex. Studios through two-bedrooms; some second-floor units sit above a gym and get bass noise.

buildings.name: 110 Horatio Street
buildings.note: Doorman mid-rise with high ceilings, near the south end of the High Line.

buildings.name: The Printing House
buildings.note: Condo on Hudson with a full health club on site. Rentals come through individual owners.

buildings.name: 756 Washington
buildings.note: Small doorman building at the High Line's southern end. No-frills, well-run.

buildings.name: 56 Seventh Avenue
buildings.note: One of the few genuine high-rises in the West Village. Doorman and gym, on a busy avenue.

buildings.name: 780 Greenwich Street
buildings.note: Post-war landmark mid-rise on a quiet Greenwich Street block.

buildings.name: 95 Christopher Street
buildings.note: Pre-war landmark doorman high-rise in the middle of Christopher Street.

buildings.name: 101 West 15th Street
buildings.note: Studios and one-bedrooms only, in the former St. Vincent's staff housing. Every unit has a balcony or terrace and in-unit laundry.

buildings.name: The Westminster
buildings.note: Related-managed, smoke-free, in the heart of Chelsea with the West Village and Flatiron each ten minutes away.

buildings.name: Chelsea Landmark
buildings.note: Sits where Chelsea, NoMad and Flatiron meet. Attended garage, building-wide Wi-Fi, and one of the better roof decks in the city.

buildings.name: The Arthur
buildings.note: Renovated Art Deco that kept its generous pre-war floor plans — the best space-per-dollar bet in Chelsea.

buildings.name: The Tate
buildings.note: Two towers in the gallery district, Ismael Leyva with Rockwell Group interiors. Oak parquet floors, oversized windows.

buildings.name: Ten23
buildings.note: Right on the High Line with a CVS in the base. Floor-to-ceiling windows; residents flag recurring elevator problems.

buildings.name: The Caledonia
buildings.note: On the High Line with a bamboo garden level. Courtyard-facing units get noticeably less light — ask for an exposure.

buildings.name: AVA High Line
buildings.note: Big, LEED-certified, and consistently well-reviewed. Far west, so the blocks empty out completely after dark.

buildings.name: Avalon West Chelsea
buildings.note: Sister building to AVA next door, on Eleventh Ave. Same staff and standards, same after-dark quiet.

buildings.name: Abington House
buildings.note: Related's High Line tower at the Hudson Yards edge — pool, bowling alley, multiple roof decks. Only a few floorplans are truly spacious.

buildings.name: Highline 537
buildings.note: Small low-rise doorman building in the gallery blocks. Gym, and not much else.

buildings.name: The Chelsea Grande
buildings.note: Landmark-district building in far west Chelsea, faced in sand-mold brick to match the block.

buildings.name: Port 10
buildings.note: Doorman high-rise on Tenth Ave, north end of the gallery district.

buildings.name: London Terrace Gardens
buildings.note: Pre-war complex spanning a full block, with a pool and garage shared across ten interior buildings. Roughly 900 rental units total.

buildings.name: Maverick Chelsea
buildings.note: Wellness-themed hybrid rental-condo tower from HAP/DXA Studio, with a 60-foot lap pool and a facaded diamond pattern.

buildings.name: Ruby Chelsea
buildings.note: COOKFOX-designed two-tower development named for fashion designer Ruby Bailey. 30% of units are affordable under Affordable NY.

buildings.name: Chelsea Canvas
buildings.note: Spans the full block between 23rd and 24th St, with a ground-floor Target. 12-foot ceilings and white oak finishes throughout.

buildings.name: Instrata Gramercy
buildings.note: The tall modern option in Gramercy. Doorman and gym, with unusually consistent praise for the building staff.

buildings.name: Gramercy Starck
buildings.note: Philippe Starck-designed condo on the Gramercy/Murray Hill edge. Rentals come through owners, so inventory is sporadic.

buildings.name: Park 23
buildings.note: Turn-of-the-century doorman high-rise on Park Avenue South, a block from Gramercy Park itself.

buildings.name: Hatten House
buildings.note: Post-war high-rise near Stuyvesant Square, walking distance to Union Square.

buildings.name: Gramercy Court
buildings.note: Pre-war doorman high-rise directly east of Gramercy Park.

buildings.name: Gramercy East
buildings.note: Post-war mid-rise; some units have the high ceilings the pre-war stock is known for.

buildings.name: New Amsterdam
buildings.note: Large post-war doorman high-rise on E 23rd, at the Gramercy/Kips Bay line.

buildings.name: The Washington Irving House
buildings.note: Post-war high-rise steps from Union Square, with a garage. Among the most transit-convenient on this list.

buildings.name: 245 East 19th Street
buildings.note: Big post-war doorman building on a quiet residential block near the park.

buildings.name: 210 East 22nd Street
buildings.note: Doorman mid-rise with high ceilings; rent includes heat, hot water and cooking gas.

buildings.name: Gemma Gramercy
buildings.note: Hill West's first Passive House project — triple-glazed windows, continuous air barrier, and energy-recovery ventilation in every unit.

buildings.name: 55 Thompson
buildings.note: Boutique tower with gas fireplaces and private balconies in select units; reviews consistently single out the concierge and resident manager as unusually responsive for a building this small.

buildings.name: 261 Hudson
buildings.note: Unusually large for the neighborhood — most SoHo doorman buildings top out under 50 units. Technically West SoHo/Hudson Square; the Equinox-curated fitness center is a real differentiator.

buildings.name: 111 Varick
buildings.note: Newest build in the group (leased up 2020) and the tallest tower here by far with real skyline/river views — a rare ground-up rental in a submarket dominated by office conversions and condos.

buildings.name: 70 Charlton
buildings.note: A condo where owners rent out units rather than a pure rental; one of downtown's few buildings with an indoor 60-foot saltwater pool.

buildings.name: 505 Greenwich Street
buildings.note: Built 2003–04, so finishes read a bit dated next to newer Hudson Square towers, but the pet spa and meditation garden are genuinely uncommon extras for a mid-size building.

buildings.name: The Greenwich Street Project
buildings.note: Winka Dubbeldam-designed hybrid of a 1915 brick warehouse and a glass-and-steel addition; punches above its 25-unit size with a resistance pool, but sits on the SoHo/Tribeca/West Village seam.

buildings.name: 40 Mercer Residences
buildings.note: Andre Balazs/Jean Nouvel-designed landmark with some of the highest per-square-foot prices in the neighborhood; most owners hold long-term, so actual rental availability is rare.

buildings.name: One Kenmare Square
buildings.note: Andre Balazs/Richard Gluckman's curved brick-and-glass facade sits right at the SoHo/Nolita/Little Italy crossroads; boutique scale means service feels personal but turnover is slow.

buildings.name: 11 Greene Street
buildings.note: Newer purpose-built rental (leased up ~2021) rather than a loft conversion despite the loft-inspired interiors; the cold-storage package room is a practical, non-marketing amenity.

buildings.name: 68 Spring Street
buildings.note: Tiny 2022 infill building; listed as "doorman + virtual doorman," suggesting coverage isn't a traditional live 24h desk — worth confirming staffing hours.

buildings.name: Renwick Modern
buildings.note: Philip Johnson/Alan Ritchie-designed condo, one of Johnson's last projects. Doorman coverage is only 8am–midnight, and with 17 units total, rentals are infrequent.

buildings.name: Independence Plaza
buildings.note: Built in 1974 as Mitchell-Lama affordable housing, because Tribeca was too undesirable then for market-rate tenants; it exited the program in 2004 and some original rent-stabilized tenants still live alongside market renters.

buildings.name: Tribeca House
buildings.note: Two connected Related-managed rental buildings (50 Murray St and 53 Park Place) run as one leasing community; popular with FiDi commuters for proximity to multiple subway lines.

buildings.name: Barclay Tower
buildings.note: Glenwood-managed high-rise with a 50-foot indoor lap pool; reviews consistently praise the doormen and cleanliness but knock the leasing office as slow on renewal terms.

buildings.name: Tribeca Tower
buildings.note: Related-managed tower with a Rockwell Group-designed lobby, a few blocks from the courthouses and City Hall — draws a lot of lawyer and finance-industry renters.

buildings.name: Truffles Tribeca
buildings.note: Twin towers linked by a glass skywalk; some tenant reviews cite lingering water-damage complaints from Hurricane Sandy and an extra $80/month gym fee.

buildings.name: 89 Murray Street
buildings.note: SOM-designed (2007) with Victoria Hagan interiors — a notably higher design pedigree than most rental buildings. Whole Foods and Barnes & Noble are at sister building 101 Warren, not on-site here.

buildings.name: 88 Leonard Street
buildings.note: Well-reviewed for cleanliness and friendly doormen, but several tenants note there's no on-site gym or in-unit laundry despite the full-amenity marketing.

buildings.name: 456 Washington Street
buildings.note: Quieter, smaller-scale rental on a cobblestoned block near the Hudson, less flashy than the Duane/Murray Street towers but with comparable full-service staffing.

buildings.name: 440 Washington Street
buildings.note: One of the smallest full-service rental buildings in the neighborhood, favored by renters who want doorman service without a high-rise's scale.

buildings.name: 101 Warren Street
buildings.note: SOM-designed condo tower famous for its rooftop "forest" of 101 Austrian pine trees and a retail podium with Whole Foods and Barnes & Noble; individual units come up for rent regularly despite condo ownership.

buildings.name: 111 Murray Street
buildings.note: One of Tribeca's newest ultra-luxury condos (2016), with a 75-foot lap pool and hammam spa; rentals here run expensive since owners treat units as investment rentals.

buildings.name: 56 Leonard Street
buildings.note: Herzog & de Meuron-designed with cantilevered, stacked floors that earned it the "Jenga" nickname — the tallest residential building in Tribeca, though overwhelmingly for-sale with only occasional high-end rentals.

buildings.name: Woolworth Tower Residences
buildings.note: Occupies the top 30 floors of the landmark 1913 Woolworth Building, with its own residential entrance; the basement pool commissioned by F.W. Woolworth himself was restored by designer Thierry Despont. Only 32 units total.

buildings.name: 200 Chambers Street
buildings.note: One of the larger condo towers on Tribeca's western edge near Hudson River Park, notable for its bright skylit indoor pool.

buildings.name: Reade Chambers
buildings.note: Small boutique condo conversion with a dedicated pet-grooming station — an unusually specific amenity for how pet-focused Tribeca's boutique buildings have become.

buildings.name: River Lofts
buildings.note: Loft-style conversion retaining exposed industrial character; a good example of the boutique, lower-rise doorman tier that coexists with Tribeca's newer glass towers.

buildings.name: The Ice House
buildings.note: Converted former cold-storage warehouse, hence the name; a mid-size boutique doorman condo just off North Moore's landmarked block.

buildings.name: 91 Leonard Street
buildings.note: Full-amenity boutique condo directly across from the much taller 56 Leonard "Jenga" tower, offering a similar service tier at a smaller, less architecturally showy scale.

buildings.name: Gateway Plaza
buildings.note: The first residential development in Battery Park City (1983), a six-building complex developed by LeFrak, Fisher Brothers, and Olnick; its gated plazas and sheer scale make it feel more like a self-contained campus.

buildings.name: Liberty House
buildings.note: Its "Terrace Club" amenity floor has a riverfront gym and pool with a retractable sun roof; direct access to the Hudson River esplanade is the bigger draw here than the interiors, which reviewers call dated.

buildings.name: Le Rivage
buildings.note: A landmarked 1929 Art Deco office tower, built on spec before the 1929 crash, converted to apartments in 1997; the pre-war bones set it apart from BPC's mostly modern glass towers.

buildings.name: Tribeca Pointe
buildings.note: Despite the Tribeca-adjacent name, this Rockrose-developed 1998 tower sits at BPC's northern tip; residents frequently cite unusually helpful staff, and units have been getting rolling renovations.

buildings.name: Riverwatch
buildings.note: A red-brick, mid-rise 1999 building at BPC's southern end; less glassy than the Hudson-facing towers, but full-service with a private courtyard.

buildings.name: South Cove Plaza
buildings.note: Sister building to Riverwatch just across the street with nearly identical stats — worth comparing both since brokers sometimes conflate them.

buildings.name: The Solaire
buildings.note: Completed in 2003, it was the first LEED Gold-certified residential high-rise in the US, using an in-building wastewater recycling system — a genuinely early and serious green building.

buildings.name: Tribeca Green
buildings.note: LEED Gold certified Related rental at BPC's north end, near Stuyvesant High School and Rockefeller Park — popular with families given the nearby schools and playgrounds.

buildings.name: Tribeca Park
buildings.note: Related-managed waterfront rental with a notably large 60-foot heated pool and a landscaped sculpture garden, distinguishing it amenity-wise from its Related siblings nearby.

buildings.name: Tribeca Bridge Tower
buildings.note: Glenwood-managed rental named for the pedestrian bridge connecting it over West Street to the Hudson River esplanade, letting residents reach the waterfront without crossing traffic.

buildings.name: The Verdesian
buildings.note: Opened in 2006 as the first US residential high-rise to achieve Platinum LEED certification; it remains one of the more genuinely energy-efficient buildings in a neighborhood full of "green" marketing claims.

buildings.name: 22 River Terrace
buildings.note: Straightforward full-service rental at BPC's northern edge near the other Related/Tribeca-named towers; less architecturally distinctive but with the same waterfront-esplanade access.

buildings.name: Liberty Court
buildings.note: The tallest of the Liberty-branded condo towers and one of the largest buildings in BPC by unit count; panoramic Hudson views come with correspondingly higher density.

buildings.name: Liberty Terrace
buildings.note: Part of the four-building Liberty complex along Rector Place; individual condo units regularly cycle onto the rental market via Milford Management and other agents.

buildings.name: Liberty View
buildings.note: Managed for rentals by Milford Management even though it's condo-owned, making it one of the more consistently available Liberty-branded buildings for renters rather than buyers.

buildings.name: Liberty Luxe
buildings.note: Newer (2009-era) addition to the Liberty complex at BPC's north end, paired architecturally with sister tower Liberty Green next door.

buildings.name: Liberty Green
buildings.note: Twin building to Liberty Luxe, marketed together as an eco-conscious pair; Milford Management runs both for rentals despite the condo ownership structure.

buildings.name: The Visionaire
buildings.note: LEED Platinum-certified (2008, Pelli Clarke Pelli design) with an in-building wastewater treatment system and solar panels — one of the most technically "green" buildings in Manhattan, not just a marketing label.

buildings.name: Riverhouse
buildings.note: LEED Gold building that also houses the Poets House library and a public library branch on its ground floor — an unusual cultural pairing, and known informally as something of a quiet celebrity enclave.

buildings.name: The Ritz-Carlton Residences
buildings.note: Condo residences stacked above a 311-room Ritz-Carlton hotel at BPC's southern tip; residents can access hotel room service, housekeeping, and spa — true hotel-branded living, at a correspondingly high common-charge cost.

buildings.name: The Regatta
buildings.note: Built in 1988, one of BPC's older condo buildings, with a distinctive year-round interior garden at the lobby level rather than the glassy modern lobbies typical of newer BPC towers.

buildings.name: Millennium Tower Residences
buildings.note: NYC's original LEED Gold-certified luxury condo, adjacent to the Ritz-Carlton complex at BPC's southern tip; notably lacks a pool despite its otherwise full amenity package.

buildings.name: The Soundings
buildings.note: A smaller, lower-rise condo on Rector Place known for unusually spacious 3- and 4-bedroom layouts with Statue of Liberty and Hudson views.

buildings.name: New York by Gehry
buildings.note: Frank Gehry's rippling stainless-steel tower was briefly the tallest residential building in the Western Hemisphere; despite the pedigree, recent building-violation records show recurring rodent complaints and inconsistent management.

buildings.name: Twenty Exchange
buildings.note: Former 1931 Art Deco headquarters of City Bank-Farmers Trust, a Citigroup predecessor; Metro Loft converted the upper floors to apartments in the 1990s, making it one of downtown's earliest office-to-residential conversions.

buildings.name: One Wall Street
buildings.note: Macklowe's 2023 conversion of Ralph Walker's 1931 Art Deco "cathedral of banking" is one of the largest office-to-residential conversions in NYC history; rent includes a Life Time Fitness membership across the building's 77,000 sq ft club.

buildings.name: 70 Pine
buildings.note: Rose Associates converted the former Cities Service/AIG Building (1932) into rentals; the screening room and bowling lanes sit inside the tower's historic bank vault, a genuinely unusual reuse of the original architecture.

buildings.name: 90 West
buildings.note: Cass Gilbert's 1907 Gothic landmark was badly damaged by falling debris on 9/11, then underwent a $148M restoration before reopening as rentals in 2005 — one of the few genuinely pre-war conversions in FiDi.

buildings.name: 200 Water Street
buildings.note: Rockrose's 1997 conversion of a 1971 office tower was NYC's first postwar office-to-residential rental conversion. Reviewers like the maintenance and doormen but flag steep year-over-year rent increases.

buildings.name: 180 Water Street
buildings.note: A well-reviewed, clean building overall, but multiple tenants cite thin walls and noise from neighbors as a recurring downside.

buildings.name: 2 Gold Street
buildings.note: One of the few FiDi rentals with a genuine indoor pool and solarium; reviewers say the pool and gym are on the small side but rarely overcrowded.

buildings.name: 63 Wall Street
buildings.note: Converted from a 1929 building in 2002; has a resident-only "speakeasy" lounge called The Transcript. Reviews are mixed — friendly staff, but small units and occasional pest complaints.

buildings.name: 100 Maiden Lane
buildings.note: Reviews run notably mixed-to-negative with recurring plumbing and construction-noise complaints; one reviewer said a comparable nearby building was nicer at the same price with none of the headache.

buildings.name: 10 Hanover Square
buildings.note: Consistently rates higher on resident-satisfaction sites than several FiDi peers, with tenants citing fast maintenance turnaround and multi-year tenancies as a sign of genuine livability.

buildings.name: 19 Dutch Street
buildings.note: Developed by Carmel Partners with 97 of its 483 units set aside as affordable housing under the same roof as market-rate rentals; residents consistently praise security and cleanliness.

buildings.name: The Broad Exchange Building
buildings.note: An 1902 Clinton & Russell landmark that was once the city's most valuable office building due to its Stock Exchange proximity; converted to rentals in 1997, then partly to condos in 2019.

buildings.name: Liberty Plaza
buildings.note: A Glenwood Management building purpose-built as residential rather than an office conversion, which reviewers say translates to fewer units per floor and a quieter, more private feel than most FiDi towers.

buildings.name: 7 Dey
buildings.note: Sits directly above the Fulton Street Transit Center, about as subway-connected as it gets downtown; reviewers like the quiet and water pressure but note the attended lobby has limited practical control over visitor access.

buildings.name: Ocean
buildings.note: A 1902 Henry Hardenbergh landmark, originally the Whitehall Building and home to a maritime club, converted to rentals by Moinian in 1999; sits at the harbor's edge with Statue of Liberty views from water-facing units.

buildings.name: 116 John Street
buildings.note: Well-reviewed for cleanliness and staff, but tenants report steep renewal increases — one cited a $500 jump after year one and roughly $1,000/month premium for declining to resign.

buildings.name: 45 Wall Street
buildings.note: Unusual for FiDi in having an actual half basketball court; reviewers praise the amenity-rich penthouse club but complain many units are dark due to surrounding buildings.

buildings.name: 37 Wall Street
buildings.note: A turn-of-the-century conversion with a genuinely clubby amenity mezzanine — library, billiards, screening room. One recurring resident tip: avoid the lower floors, which get less light and more street noise.

buildings.name: 95 Wall
buildings.note: Designed with interiors by Yoo (Philippe Starck's brand), down to crystal chandeliers in the kitchens. Complaints center on inconsistent elevator reliability and thin-wall noise between units.

buildings.name: 75 Wall Street
buildings.note: A condo building with individual units cycling onto the rental market, and one of FiDi's more dramatic 360-degree rooftop lounges; sits right at the Wall/Water Street corner near the Fulton St transit hub.

buildings.name: Bridgeview House
buildings.note: A 1962-built condo/rental hybrid between Elizabeth Street and the Bowery — one of very few genuinely staffed buildings in the historic Chinatown core, where most stock is walk-up tenements.

buildings.name: Hester Gardens
buildings.note: Built in 2004, unusually new for this stretch of Chinatown, with a second-floor landscaped garden that's a rare private-outdoor perk in this part of the neighborhood.

buildings.name: One Manhattan Square
buildings.note: Extell's East River supertall is Two Bridges' most famous — and most contested — building, having drawn lawsuits over its shadow on the LES waterfront; its 100,000-sq-ft amenity floor reads more like a resort than a typical rental building.

buildings.name: 247 Cherry Street
buildings.note: JDS Development/SHoP Architects' green terra-cotta supertall opened in 2025 as a mixed-income building — roughly a quarter of the units are permanently affordable under the same roof as market-rate rentals, unusual for a tower this tall.

buildings.name: The Crossroads
buildings.note: A modest, low-key doorman rental that predates Two Bridges' 2020s supertall boom; some sources classify it as Chinatown instead since it sits right on the border near Rutgers Street.

buildings.name: 1 University Place
buildings.note: Sits directly across from Washington Square Park; corner units reportedly have 18-foot ceilings and marble fireplaces. No gym — doorman-and-laundry only, unusually bare for a building this size.

buildings.name: The Greenwich
buildings.note: 1905 department-store conversion; one of the few genuinely full-amenity rentals in the neighborhood's low-rise core, a short walk from the New School.

buildings.name: 24 Fifth Avenue
buildings.note: Emery Roth-designed 1926 former hotel. Legally a co-op, but it's run almost entirely as no-fee rentals by the Brodsky Organization — in practice one of GV's biggest true doorman inventories.

buildings.name: 25 Fifth Avenue
buildings.note: The only pre-war condo on lower Fifth's "Gold Coast," a block off Washington Square. Wood-burning fireplaces in many units — unusual for a building with active rental turnover.

buildings.name: Devonshire House
buildings.note: Another Emery Roth pre-war (1928) with a landscaped courtyard residents call one of the best private outdoor spaces in the Village. Condo — most owners hold rather than lease, so listings are sparse.

buildings.name: 11 Waverly Place
buildings.note: Steps from Washington Square and NYU, so it skews young. Staff gets consistent praise in reviews; slow work-order response from management is the recurring complaint.

buildings.name: 2 Fifth Avenue
buildings.note: The big curved-driveway tower on the north corner of Washington Square, with a 30-person staff. Co-op — what's available to renters comes as furnished shareholder sublets requiring board approval.

buildings.name: 1 Fifth Avenue
buildings.note: Art Deco 1927 landmark with some of the best Washington Square/skyline views downtown. Same caveat as 2 Fifth — a co-op, so rentals happen via shareholder sublease.

buildings.name: The Villager
buildings.note: Small 1902 conversion across from the old Jefferson Market Courthouse, with wood-burning fireplaces and exposed brick. Doorman coverage is part-time only — the weakest full-service claim on this list.

buildings.name: 7W21
buildings.note: Morris Adjmi-designed 2016 Rose Associates building steps from Madison Square Park. Deep amenity list — golf simulator, foosball, media room — but no pool, which residents say they wish it had.

buildings.name: Echelon Chelsea
buildings.note: Rare in this district for having an actual clubhouse pool. Trade-off is noise — 21st Street nightlife makes front-facing units loud.

buildings.name: Vanguard Chelsea
buildings.note: LEED Platinum with a genuinely unusual amenity — an herb garden on the roof deck. Reviews are split on management, with steep renewal increases a recurring complaint.

buildings.name: The Capitol at Chelsea
buildings.note: Despite the "at Chelsea" branding it actually sits on the NoMad/Flatiron line — one of several buildings here whose marketing name doesn't match its real cross streets.

buildings.name: The Grand Madison
buildings.note: 1906 Brunswick Hotel conversion with old-school white-glove touches like in-house dry cleaning. Condo building, so rental inventory depends on individual owners listing.

buildings.name: Flatiron 18
buildings.note: Solid 2005 post-war infill between Fifth and Sixth. No standout amenity — the reliable but unglamorous option on this list, priced accordingly.

buildings.name: The Caroline
buildings.note: Largest rental building in the immediate district. The "pool" is actually a paid Life Time/NYHRC club membership, not an included amenity — trips up people expecting it free.

buildings.name: The Stanford
buildings.note: A genuinely 42-story tower off Madison Square Park — taller than people expect, since most listing sites file it under NoMad. Condo building.

buildings.name: Flatiron House
buildings.note: COOKFOX-designed 2023 building, two towers linked by a planted garden and glass walkway. Mostly for-sale, so rental inventory is thin and expensive when it appears.

buildings.name: Bank of the Metropolis
buildings.note: Landmarked 1903 bank building whose original board included Tiffany, Steinway and Sloane. Loft-like high ceilings, but amenities beyond the doorman are minimal.

buildings.name: 15 Union Square West
buildings.note: Former Tiffany & Co. headquarters, reborn 2008 with a genuine 50-foot lap pool and spa. Condo, so rental stock is limited.

buildings.name: 800 Sixth Avenue
buildings.note: 16-foot ceilings and curved bay windows; technically closer to 27th/28th St than the Flatiron core, but shows up in most neighborhood round-ups and staff get consistently good reviews.

buildings.name: 1 Union Square South
buildings.note: Related-managed; its north facade carries the Metronome public art clock. Reviews call the roof "never crowded" but flag that corner units run cold in winter.
